source.title: On the Generalization of Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum
source.authors: Ali Ramezani-Kebrya; Kimon Antonakopoulos; V. Cevher; Ashish J. Khisti; Ben Liang

record.tranche_reason: Reports theoretical stability/generalization results and experiments on momentum schedules and training/test error, using different interventions and measures from the claim's mapped original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper tests momentum schedule and related generalization behavior. It does not test random-label memorization, width scaling, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, adaptive optimizers, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Cited prior work is not recorded as study results. Figure-only sweeps are recorded without reconstructing values.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes heavy-ball momentum duration, stability bounds, and natural-label classification performance. None of its own results tests V1–V8. SGD and SGDM are not adaptive optimizers as named in V4; Adam comparisons are cited prior work, and extending the analysis to Adam is future work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors establish conditional stability-based generalization bounds for appropriately scheduled early momentum and for projected SGDM under strongly convex losses with restricted hyperparameters. An unbounded stability gap does not itself prove failure to generalize. Their experiments favor early momentum on tested nonconvex tasks; on ImageNet, the clearest reported improvement is a smaller generalization gap, with validation loss essentially unchanged.
record.recipe_differences: Studies heavy-ball momentum and a modified early-momentum schedule; the experiments use natural-label classification and measure test error/generalization gap, not the versions' defining interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Momentum duration, momentum parameter, loss regime (nonconvex versus strongly convex), dataset size, and training duration change reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Early momentum can improve nonconvex test performance; Table 1 reports test loss 0.2892 for SGDEM, 0.3194 for SGDM, and 0.3596 for SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An appropriately chosen early-momentum schedule can improve held-out performance over constant momentum and vanilla SGD in the tested nonconvex classification settings.

fits_no_version.finding: For ResNet-18 on ImageNet, applying momentum for 50 of 90 epochs minimizes the reported generalization gap; validation loss remains essentially unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Momentum duration can change the training–validation gap without materially changing validation loss.

fits_no_version.finding: In regularized logistic regression, momentum improves training performance but increases generalization gaps at sufficiently large sample sizes; its test-performance benefit diminishes with longer training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested strongly convex settings, momentum's optimization advantage can be offset by an increased generalization gap.

record.problems: Most experimental results are figure-only with no tabulated numeric values in the supplied text. The core theoretical claims rely on uniform stability, which the authors note is sufficient rather than necessary for generalization. Empirical evidence covers a limited set of datasets and architectures; random-label fitting and the claim versions' defining mechanisms are not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out; the reported relevant experiments fit within the 60-row limit. Cited prior-work results were excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Width scaling beyond zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, small-data regimes, underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removal of highly memorized examples compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: T6 is relative to these eight specific versions, despite the paper's direct study of generalization more broadly. No verdict labels are warranted. All row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; this does not negate the paper's stated momentum effects.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width scaling beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Large versus small batch generalization under epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a correlate of the generalization gap.
Removing examples that are most memorized and measuring test accuracy.
